items.issuing_body: Federal Trade Commission
items.title: FTC policy statement text: the Commission will no longer pursue disparate-impact claims in any context and will bring no antidiscrimination claims under Section 5, while the statement disclaims binding effect
items.facts: The FTC "Policy Statement Regarding Disparate-Impact Claims and 'Unfair Discrimination' Claims," listed in the FTC Legal Library under date August 7, 2026, states in its Introduction: "The FTC has previously pursued disparate-impact claims in two contexts: under Section 5 of the FTC Act (where they have been styled as 'unfair discrimination' claims), and under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act ('ECOA'). In both instances, the FTC acted ultra vires. Section 5 contains no antidiscrimination cause of action, let alone a disparate-impact one. And while ECOA does prohibit intentional discrimination, it does not authorize disparate-impact claims." It concludes: "Accordingly, in light of (1) the FTC's lack of statutory authority to bring disparate-impact claims and (2) the fundamental legal and policy defects of disparate-impact liability laid out in President Trump's executive order, the FTC will no longer pursue disparate-impact claims in any context. In addition, because Section 5 does not create an antidiscrimination cause of action, the Commission will not bring any such claims under Section 5." The statement identifies the order as "Exec. Order No. 14281, Restoring Equality of Opportunity and Meritocracy, 90 Fed. Reg. 17537 (Apr. 23, 2025)" and says it directs agencies, including the FTC, to "deprioritize enforcement of all statutes and regulations to the extent they include disparate-impact liability." On what survives, the statement says "Intentional discrimination can be combatted through traditional disparate-treatment claims, and the Commission remains firmly committed to bringing such claims where the law allows," citing a July 17, 2025 concurring statement in the Asbury Automotive Group matter (Matter No. 2223135) stating the Commission "will not hesitate to bring disparate-treatment claims under ECOA where the facts support such claims." Footnote 1 states: "This Policy Statement does not confer any rights on any person and does not operate to bind the FTC or the public. In any enforcement action, the Commission must prove the challenged act or practice violates one or more existing statutory or regulatory requirements. In addition, this Policy Statement does not preempt federal, state, or local laws. Compliance with those laws, however, will not necessarily preclude Commission law enforcement action under the FTC Act or other statutes." The same footnote records that the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs designated the Policy Statement as not a "major rule" as defined by 5 U.S.C. 804(2). The quoted passages are taken from the Introduction and the opening of Part II of the document; the remainder of the document was not read.

items.title: Senate will not vote on the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act before its August recess; Majority Leader says a vote comes when the Senate returns September 14
items.facts: As reported by CoinDesk on August 7, 2026, "the U.S. Senate will not vote on the crypto market structure bill before it breaks for the rest of the month," with industry participants still expecting a vote in September. CoinDesk reports that Senate Majority Leader John Thune confirmed through a spokesperson that there would not be a vote on the Clarity Act in August but that there would be one the following month, quoting the statement: "The Dems are insistent on no Clarity vote... I worked with sponsors of the bill. [Senator Cynthia Lummis] was great, and we're getting that queued up first thing when we come back." Per the same report, the Senate returns to Washington on September 14, 2026; its remaining scheduled business before recess is a continuing resolution to fund the federal government, a Russia sanctions bill and a group of nominations; the Clarity Act had no time agreement limiting debate; the bill would require 60 votes to advance; and the outstanding issues include an ethics provision, Agriculture Committee provisions and law-enforcement concerns. The bill, H.R. 3633, previously received independent approvals from the Senate Banking Committee and the Senate Agriculture Committee. CoinDesk credits Politico with first reporting the expected absence of a pre-recess vote.
items.source_label: CoinDesk — "Senate won't vote on crypto Clarity Act before its summer break," published August 7, 2026 (media coverage; no official primary record exists for an absence of scheduled floor action)

items.issuing_body: Commodity Futures Trading Commission
items.title: CFTC proposed rule "Conflicts and Affiliations" published in the Federal Register; comments due October 5, 2026
items.facts: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission's proposed rule "Conflicts and Affiliations" was published in the Federal Register on August 6, 2026 as document 2026-15948, RIN 3038-AF76. The published document states that the Commission "is proposing new rules and amendments to its existing regulations for futures commission merchants (‘FCMs’), swap execution facilities (‘SEFs’), designated contract markets (‘DCMs’), and derivatives clearing organizations (‘DCOs’)" and that the proposal "addresses requirements relating to financial oversight of FCMs by self-regulatory organizations (‘SROs’) and designated self-regulatory organizations (‘DSROs’), as well as disclosure requirements by FCMs regarding affiliate relationships that an FCM has with a SEF, DCM, or DCO." For SEFs, DCMs and DCOs, the document states the proposal "would also establish requirements, including conflicts of interest rules, to address those registered entities' relationships with certain affiliates, such as FCM affiliates and affiliated principal trading firms," and includes guidance on safeguards to protect the impartiality of SEFs, DCMs and DCOs, addressing "the sharing of resources including staffing, technology, and office space, and limitations on the sharing of non-public information." The DATES section states: "Comments must be in writing and received by October 5, 2026." Comments are to be identified by "Conflicts and Affiliations" and RIN 3038-AF76.

items.facts: Ludlow Exchange, LLC d/b/a Novig filed a complaint for declaratory and injunctive relief in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York on August 5, 2026 (Case 1:26-cv-06676, Document 3) against New York Attorney General Letitia James, New York State Gaming Commission Executive Director Robert Williams, Chair Brian O'Dwyer, and the Commission's commissioners, each sued in an official capacity. items.issuing_body: New York State Department of Financial Services
items.title: NYDFS settles with money transmitter Order Express for $250,000 over cybersecurity regulation violations
items.facts: The New York State Department of Financial Services announced on August 5, 2026 that Order Express, Inc., a licensed money transmitter, will pay a $250,000 penalty for violations of the Department's cybersecurity regulation, 23 NYCRR Part 500. According to the Department, its investigators identified deficiencies in the company's cybersecurity program and controls required under the regulation, including a failure to maintain adequate cybersecurity policies for system updates and inadequate risk assessments. The Department states that Order Express has remediated the deficiencies identified by the investigation, and that based on its limited revenue Order Express is exempt from many of Part 500's requirements. The announcement notes that the Part 500 regulation took effect in March 2017 with an amendment effective November 2023.

items.issuing_body: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York (DOJ)
items.title: SDNY indicts NFT startup founder for securities and wire fraud over a $10 million SAFT raise
items.facts: The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York announced on August 5, 2026 (Press Release 26-231) that Taj Tarsha, founder of Few and Far Limited, "has been indicted for securities and wire fraud for defrauding investors of the crypto startup he founded by making false and misleading statements regarding the use of investor funds and subsequently misappropriating those funds." According to the release, beginning in February 2022 Tarsha solicited investments through Simple Agreements for Future Tokens (SAFTs), under which investors paid upfront for rights to receive FAR tokens at a later date, and "raised over $10 million from the sale of 95 million FAR tokens to at least 67 investors." The offering materials promised that funds would be used to advance development of a decentralized marketplace for non-fungible tokens. The release states that "almost immediately" Tarsha began misappropriating investor funds for personal use "including gambling at an online casino and purchasing speculative cryptocurrencies," that a June 2023 audit uncovered the misappropriation, and that when the FAR token launched in May 2024 "it was effectively worthless and soon ceased trading." Tarsha, 34, of Miami, Florida, was arrested on June 6, 2026; the case is assigned to U.S. District Judge Lewis A. Kaplan; each charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. The Office states that "the charges contained in the Indictment are merely accusations, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty."
items.source_label: U.S. Department of Justice — U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York, Press Release 26-231, August 5, 2026

items.issuing_body: U.S. Department of the Treasury
items.title: Treasury publishes U.S.-UK Financial Regulatory Working Group joint statement recording US update on GENIUS Act stablecoin implementation
items.facts: The U.S. Department of the Treasury published on August 4, 2026 the joint statement of the 13th meeting of the UK-U.S. Financial Regulatory Working Group, hosted by HM Treasury in London on July 8, 2026. The statement records that U.S. Treasury and HM Treasury officials were joined by representatives of the Bank of England, the Financial Conduct Authority, the Federal Reserve Board, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Securities and Exchange Commission. It states that authorities provided updates on their respective regulatory regimes for digital assets, including stablecoins, and on their work to modernize payment services more broadly, and that U.S. authorities provided an update on implementing the GENIUS Act for stablecoins and on digital asset market structure. The discussion also covered the G20 Cross-border Payments Roadmap and priorities for tokenisation. The statement records that the U.S.-UK Transatlantic Taskforce for Markets of the Future announced initial recommendations on July 14 along with a U.S.-UK joint statement on stablecoins, and that the Working Group plans to reconvene in early 2027.

items.issuing_body: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
items.title: SEC settles Blazar Token crypto offering-fraud case with a permanent conduct-based injunction and $681,105 in disgorgement offset by criminal restitution
items.facts: SEC Litigation Release No. 26599, dated August 4, 2026, states that on August 4, 2026 the SEC filed a consent and proposed final judgment in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey as to John A. DeSalvo, a former New Jersey corrections officer, in an action alleging "crypto offering and investment fraud schemes." The release states that the Commission's August 2023 complaint alleges DeSalvo "fraudulently raised at least $623,888 from approximately 222 investors in connection with the so-called Blazar Token," and that he "claimed that the Blazar Token would replace traditional state pension systems and falsely told investors that Blazar Token was registered with the SEC; that he had arranged for Blazar Token to be purchased by automatic payroll deduction; and that investors were guaranteed to receive extraordinary returns." The complaint further alleges that in an earlier scheme beginning in late January 2021 he raised approximately $95,000 from 17 investors for a program he claimed would invest in stocks, options and crypto assets. The release states DeSalvo consented to entry of a final judgment, subject to court approval, permanently enjoining him from violating Sections 5(a), 5(c) and 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of the Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5, imposing a conduct-based injunction permanently barring him from participating in the issuance, offer or sale of any security, and ordering him liable for disgorgement of $681,105, "which shall be deemed satisfied by the order of restitution entered against him in a parallel criminal matter."
items.source_label: SEC Litigation Release No. 26599 (August 4, 2026)

items.issuing_body: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
items.title: SEC files proposed final judgment settling crypto market-manipulation and wash-trading claims against Gotbit Consulting, and dismisses claims against Fedor Kedrov
items.facts: SEC Litigation Release No. 26598, dated August 3, 2026, states that on July 28, 2026 the SEC filed a proposed final judgment in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts as to its claims against Gotbit Consulting LLC a/k/a Gotbit Hedge Fund, and that if approved the judgment "would settle the Commission's previously-filed fraud and market manipulation claims against Gotbit." The Commission previously filed a notice of voluntary dismissal as to its pending claims against Fedor Kedrov. The release states that the SEC's October 2024 complaint "alleged that Gotbit engaged in a scheme to manipulate the market for a crypto asset that was offered and sold subject to an investment contract, including by generating artificial trading volume for the crypto asset," by "self-trading (commonly referred to as 'wash trading') or by engaging in other trading practices that likewise served no economic purpose." Gotbit consented to entry of a final judgment, subject to court approval, permanently enjoining it from violating Section 17(a)(1) and (3) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Sections 9(a)(2) and 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5(a) and (c), and from participating directly or indirectly in any issuance, purchase, offer or sale of any securities. The release also states that in a parallel criminal proceeding Gotbit pleaded guilty to wire fraud and conspiracy to commit market manipulation and wire fraud, and was sentenced in June 2025 to five years' probation.

items.issuing_body: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), U.S. Department of the Treasury
items.title: FinCEN assesses a $125 million penalty against UBS Financial Services for willful Bank Secrecy Act violations, its largest ever against a broker-dealer
items.facts: On August 3, 2026 the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network assessed a $125,000,000 civil money penalty against UBS Financial Services Inc. (UBSFS) for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act. FinCEN states this is the largest penalty ever imposed against a broker-dealer for BSA violations to date, and that it is FinCEN's second enforcement action against UBSFS after a December 2018 consent order carrying a $14.5 million penalty that had also found UBSFS failed to adequately monitor foreign currency wires. FinCEN states that despite assurances it would remediate, UBSFS did not, and subsequently failed to appropriately monitor over 50,000 foreign currency wires with an aggregate value of more than $10 billion, and did not disclose these failings to FinCEN, which learned of them through an investigation opened after a regulatory examination. FinCEN also found failures to perform appropriate customer due diligence for high-risk customers with ties to Russia and Latin America, resulting in a failure to timely report hundreds of suspicious transactions. As part of the resolution UBSFS admits it willfully violated the BSA, including failing to implement and maintain an AML program and to file suspicious activity reports. The consent order requires UBSFS to work with a third party to complete a lookback for undetected suspicious transactions and to undergo an independent review of its AML program covering priority illicit finance risks that FinCEN identifies as the U.S. Southwest border, cartels and possible narcotics trafficking, Iran, Russia and Venezuela. FinCEN states it will waive up to $15 million for expenses incurred on that undertaking upon satisfactory completion. FinCEN states that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission and FINRA cooperated on the matter.
items.source_label: FinCEN news release, August 3, 2026

items.issuing_body: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
items.title: SEC censures UBS Financial Services and imposes a $20 million penalty for failing to timely file suspicious activity reports on foreign currency wires
items.facts: On August 3, 2026 the Securities and Exchange Commission instituted and settled administrative and cease-and-desist proceedings against UBS Financial Services Inc. (UBSFS) in Release No. 34-106026 and Advisers Act Release No. IA-6985, File No. 3-22665. The Commission found that UBSFS willfully violated Section 17(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17a-8 thereunder by failing to timely file certain suspicious activity reports. The order finds that from January 2019 through June 2023 UBSFS failed to adequately monitor customers' foreign currency wire transactions as required by its own anti-money laundering policies, because of flaws first in its legacy monitoring system and then in the automated system that replaced it in February 2021, and that UBSFS also failed to appropriately maintain customer risk profiles including red flags tied to high-risk jurisdictions. The order states that from January 2019 through January 2021 UBSFS failed to adequately monitor approximately 52,000 foreign currency wire transactions with a notional value of approximately $7.6 billion, and that from February 2021 through June 2023 it failed to monitor or adequately monitor more than 8,000 of approximately 190,000 such transactions, being 4 percent by count and carrying a notional value of more than $2.7 billion, being 20 percent by value. Lookback reports filed beginning in October 2023 were not timely under the SAR rule and concerned thousands of suspicious transactions totalling approximately $250 million. The Commission ordered UBSFS to cease and desist, censured it, and ordered payment of a $20 million civil money penalty within 30 days. UBSFS consented without admitting the findings, except as to admissions contained in its consent to the FinCEN assessment.
items.source_label: SEC order, Release No. 34-106026 / IA-6985, File No. 3-22665, August 3, 2026

items.issuing_body: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission
items.title: CFTC orders UBS Financial Services to pay $8 million for failing to diligently supervise AML transaction monitoring of foreign currency wires
items.facts: On August 3, 2026 the Commodity Futures Trading Commission announced, as Release 9277-26, a settled order against UBS Financial Services Inc. (UBS FSI) in CFTC Docket No. 26-04, dated July 31, 2026. The Commission found that from January 2019 through June 2023 UBS FSI, a registered futures commission merchant, failed to adequately configure and administer its anti-money laundering transaction monitoring systems for wire transfers denominated in foreign currencies and effectuated through retail customer accounts, and thereby failed to diligently supervise its business in violation of Commission Regulation 166.3. The order states that UBS FSI estimates more than 28,000 such wires with a total U.S. dollar value of at least $8.9 billion were insufficiently monitored or omitted from monitoring. It records that a manually generated report used until February 2021 did not capture scenarios such as transfers to or from high-risk jurisdictions, round dollar transactions and dormant account activity; that a coding error discovered in October 2020 had suppressed more than 400 alerts; and that after the automated system went live in March 2021 the firm configured it to draw on an intra-day feed rather than a complete end-of-day feed and did not remediate that and a transaction-labelling issue until October 2022. The order states that a violation of Regulation 166.3 is an independent violation for which no underlying violation is necessary. UBS FSI submitted an offer of settlement, admits the facts set out in the order and acknowledges that its conduct violated Regulation 166.3. The order requires UBS FSI to cease and desist and to pay an $8,000,000 civil monetary penalty within thirty days, and imposes cooperation undertakings. The CFTC release states that FinCEN, the SEC and FINRA announced related actions against UBS FSI the same day.

items.issuing_body: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (as reported)
items.title: CFTC reported to have filed an emergency motion in Manhattan federal court to stop New York applying state gambling law to Kalshi
items.facts: As reported by Al Jazeera on July 31, 2026 carrying Associated Press and Reuters copy, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission filed an emergency motion in federal court late on Thursday night to stop New York from subjecting the prediction market Kalshi to state gambling laws, describing the state's action as overreach that would irreparably harm the agency and the markets it regulates. The same report states that the CFTC has claimed exclusive jurisdiction to regulate transactions offered in prediction markets and has challenged regulatory activity in at least nine states, including New York, which it sued in April, and that on Wednesday the federal appeals court in Manhattan rejected Kalshi's request to avoid possible enforcement activity while it appeals U.S. District Judge Analisa Torres's July 8 refusal to issue an injunction against the state. The report states that Kalshi sought to move New York's action to Manhattan federal court eight hours after the attorney general filed it, and quotes Kalshi as saying that New York seeks to place itself in the position of a nationwide derivatives regulator. PYMNTS reported the same day that the CFTC has sued to stop New York's attempt to halt Kalshi's operations, and PYMNTS and NY1 both quote CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig as stating that New York seeks to force an unprecedented sudden shutdown of prediction markets nationwide and that the CFTC has already sued to stop this and will continue to defend its jurisdiction. No official CFTC press release or public statement on this filing was located on cftc.gov, and the court filing itself was not retrieved.

items.issuing_body: New York State Office of the Attorney General
items.title: New York sues KalshiEX, LLC in state court, alleging its prediction market is an unlicensed gambling operation
items.facts: On July 31, 2026, New York Governor Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James announced that New York has sued KalshiEX, LLC for running an illegal gambling operation in New York through its prediction market platform. The Office of the Attorney General states that its investigation found Kalshi's prediction market is an illegal, unlicensed gambling operation, and that the lawsuit alleges Kalshi's prediction markets meet the legal definition of gambling because the outcomes of the events users bet on are uncertain and outside the control of the bettor or hinge on a game of chance. The release states Kalshi has failed to obtain a license from the New York State Gaming Commission, and that Kalshi's markets are available to users between the ages of 18 and 20 even though New York law requires a person to be at least 21 to participate in mobile sports betting. The Attorney General is asking the court to order Kalshi to stop operating as an unlicensed gambling business, forfeit all illegal gains, distribute restitution to consumers who were harmed, and pay fines equal to three times the gains the company made. The release notes prior related New York actions, including an October 2025 New York State Gaming Commission cease-and-desist letter to Kalshi and April 2026 suits against Coinbase and Gemini over alleged illegal gambling platforms. The matter is handled by the OAG Investor Protection Bureau.
items.source_label: New York State Office of the Attorney General press release (July 31, 2026)

items.issuing_body: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission
items.title: CFTC settles manipulation charges over trading of a State of the Union event contract, with $17,569.98 disgorgement, a $17,500 penalty and a three-year trading ban
items.facts: On July 31, 2026 the Commodity Futures Trading Commission entered a settled Order Instituting Proceedings under Section 6(c) and (d) of the Commodity Exchange Act against George Anthony Devolder Santos, CFTC Docket No. 26-05, announced as CFTC Release 9276-26. The Commission found that between February 12, 2026 and February 25, 2026 Santos violated Section 6(c)(1) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. 9(1), and Regulation 180.1(a)(1), (3). The order states that KalshiEX LLC, a designated contract market, offered an event contract titled "Who will attend the State of the Union?" and a market on whether Santos would attend the 2026 State of the Union, and that Santos traded both Yes and No positions in that market while making social media statements about his attendance, exiting the No position on February 25 for a profit of $14,390.57. The order states that event contracts are a type of swap as defined by the Act, and that Santos violated Section 6(c)(1) and Regulation 180.1(a) when he traded in an event contract where he could influence the outcome of the underlying event and engaged in activity designed to affect the price of the swap. Santos consented to the order without admitting the findings or conclusions. The order requires him to cease and desist, to disgorge $17,569.98, to pay a $17,500 civil monetary penalty within thirty days, and prohibits him from trading on or subject to the rules of any registered entity for three years. KalshiEX LLC is identified in the order as the venue that listed the contract and is not a respondent.

items.issuing_body: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission
items.title: CFTC proposes conflicts-of-interest and affiliation rules for vertically integrated market structures
items.facts: On July 30, 2026, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, release 9274-26, seeking public comment on amendments to Part 37, Part 38, and Part 39 of the CFTC's regulations, as well as Commission regulations 1.52 and 1.55. The release states that the Commission has continued to observe growth in the number of affiliations between CFTC-regulated entities, including derivatives clearing organizations, designated contract markets, swap execution facilities, futures commission merchants, and other market participants such as market makers, and that in light of these developments the Commission proposes new rules and amendments to its existing regulations to address issues that may arise in connection with such firms, including with respect to perceived and potential conflicts of interest. Chairman Michael S. Selig is quoted as saying that by setting forth principles-based regulations for vertically integrated market structures, the CFTC is taking a significant step in its continued efforts to support responsible innovation in U.S. derivatives markets, and that the proposal would institute purpose-fit rules of the road that bolster market integrity without stifling novel market structures or imposing excessive compliance costs on registrants. The release states comments will be accepted for 60 days following publication in the Federal Register. As of August 2, 2026 the notice had not yet appeared in the Federal Register.
items.source_label: CFTC press release 9274-26 (July 30, 2026)

items.issuing_body: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
items.title: SEC approves amended generic listing standards for Commodity-Based Trust Shares, adding a 15% digital-commodity buffer and allowing actively managed products
items.facts: In three orders published in the Federal Register between July 30 and August 3, 2026, the Securities and Exchange Commission approved amendments to the generic listing standards for Commodity-Based Trust Shares at Nasdaq, NYSE Arca and Cboe BZX. In Release No. 34-105995 (July 27, 2026; File No. SR-NASDAQ-2026-032), the Commission approved new Nasdaq Rule 5711(d)(iv)(C), which provides that up to 15 percent of a Commodity-Based Trust Share's net asset value in the aggregate may consist of digital commodities that do not meet the existing criteria for commodities, or securities that do not meet the existing criteria for securities, with any derivative calculated on its gross notional value. The rule defines 'digital commodity' to mean a commodity that is a digital asset and is intrinsically linked to and derives its value from the programmatic operation of a functional crypto system, as well as supply and demand dynamics, rather than from the expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others. The exchanges state that this definition is informed by the joint interpretive guidance issued by the Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission published at 91 FR 13714 on March 23, 2026, and that each exchange will submit a rule filing to conform the definition if legislation is enacted defining the term. The same orders remove the requirement that Commodity-Based Trust Shares be designed to reflect the performance of one or more reference assets or an index of reference assets, which permits actively managed products to be listed under the generic standards, and add a trading-halt requirement where portfolio information is not disseminated to all market participants at the same time, together with a requirement that persons with access to non-public portfolio information be subject to procedures designed to prevent its use and dissemination. items.facts: On July 27, 2026, Judge Katherine Menendez of the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota granted KalshiEX LLC, Polymarket US, and the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission a preliminary injunction against Minnesota's law criminalizing the operation of prediction markets, ruling that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on their claim that the state law is expressly preempted by the federal Commodity Exchange Act as applied to event contracts that qualify as 'swaps.' The court wrote that plaintiffs 'have met their burden to show they are likely to succeed on the merits of their express-preemption claims, at least as to the application of Minnesota's law to many of the trades listed on Kalshi's and Polymarket US's platforms,' while noting the state ban might still reach some contracts (such as bets on entertainment outcomes) that do not qualify as swaps. The preliminary injunction remains in effect until a final decision on the merits is reached. Minnesota's law, signed May 18, 2026, was the first in the country to classify prediction-market operation as a criminal offense. items.facts: On July 24, 2026, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission's Division of Market Oversight (DMO) issued an advisory reminding designated contract markets (DCMs) about the proper procedures for submitting self-certifications of an event contract series. The advisory addresses concerns about the practice of submitting broad, template-style certifications that combine many potential event contract variations into a single certification. According to the advisory, this approach limits DMO's ability to determine whether a DCM has provided all the information, explanation, and analysis required by Commission Regulation Section 40.2, and whether it has adequately evaluated the settlement methodology, data sources, and core-principles compliance of any contract it intends to list. The guidance reiterates that broad, template-style certifications should not be submitted, and explains when closely related event contracts may be certified as a class or submitted for approval under Commission Regulations Sections 40.2(d) or 40.3. The advisory was issued as CFTC Staff Letter No. 26-22.

Six Iran-based entities comprising the Dot One conglomerate are also designated, including DotOne Gold Company, which operates Tala Token (an allegedly gold-backed digital asset token); significant quantities of Tala Token passed through Zedcex infrastructure in early 2025. items.title: Reported: New would-be-final CLARITY Act draft circulated July 22 with DOJ-enforced ethics ban on federal officials issuing digital assets
items.facts: As reported by CoinDesk on July 22, 2026 and corroborated by CNBC, Roll Call, American Banker and Disruption Banking the same day, lawmakers circulated a would-be-final draft of the Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act as the U.S. Senate prepared for floor action before its August recess. The draft includes a conflict-of-interest section barring the President, Vice President, members of Congress, federal judges and their spouses from issuing or sponsoring digital assets for pay while in office; per CNBC, the Department of Justice would enforce the ban with fines of up to $250,000 per day and disgorgement of profits plus a penalty of up to 10% of amounts received. The ethics provision is set to sunset January 20, 2029 and would require regulators to implement it within one year of enactment. Per CoinDesk, the draft retains the Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act (non-custodial developers not treated as money transmitters) and adds new language on federal preemption, provisional registration and commodity pool operators. Senate Majority Leader John Thune's office said he intends to move to floor action in the coming days; the draft text was posted at Punchbowl News but had not been shared with Democratic lawmakers, several of whom criticized the DOJ-enforced ethics mechanism. The bill needs 60 Senate votes.

items.issuing_body: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (Commissioner Hester M. Peirce)
items.title: SEC Commissioner Peirce: some crypto vaults and onchain lending strategies may fall within federal securities laws
items.facts: On July 22, 2026, SEC Commissioner Hester M. Peirce issued a statement titled 'Headstands and Summervaults: A Statement on Crypto Vaults and Lending Strategies,' stating that crypto vaults and onchain lending strategies may fall within the federal securities laws depending on how they are structured and managed. Peirce wrote that moving activities within the scope of the securities laws onchain 'as a general matter, does not take those activities outside the scope,' and that 'tokenized securities are still securities. That principle holds for vaults.' She said parties who manage vaults (for example, by selecting yield-generating activities, re-allocating assets, or selecting the parties that make those decisions) or lending strategies (for example, by setting interest rates, deciding which assets to accommodate, and setting loan-to-value limits and liquidation thresholds) may want to analyze whether their activities implicate the securities laws; that a vault could be a common enterprise or fall into investment company territory and involvement may implicate investment adviser requirements; and that onchain loans could bear the hallmarks of notes that are securities. She stated the analysis turns on the specific facts and circumstances and invited market participants to engage with the SEC. The statement is an individual Commissioner statement, not a Commission rule or enforcement action.

items.title: House Agriculture subcommittee examines prediction market customer protections and CFTC authority over sports event contracts
items.facts: The Subcommittee on Commodity Markets, Digital Assets, and Rural Development held a hearing titled 'Examining Prediction Markets: Customer Protections and Market Integrity in Sports Event Markets' on July 21, 2026, chaired by Rep. Dusty Johnson (R-SD). Five witnesses testified: Robert Schwartz (partner, Morgan Lewis; former CFTC general counsel), Carl Kennedy (derivatives attorney, Katten Muchin Rosenman), Chris Cylke (SVP government relations, American Gaming Association), David Bean (chairman, Indian Gaming Association), and Asaf Meir (co-founder and CEO, Solidus Labs). Schwartz and Kennedy defended CFTC jurisdiction under the Commodity Exchange Act; Cylke and Bean argued sports event contracts are gambling subject to state police powers and the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, with Bean urging advancement of H.R. 7840 (Event Contract Enforcement Act). Cylke cited Kalshi's sports-related trading volume exceeding $111 billion through H1 2026 and noted that 45% of all online sports betting advertising now comes from prediction market operators. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-MI) pressed witnesses on the CFTC's order directing Kalshi to defy a Michigan state court order; Schwartz described the order as extraordinary, stating: 'It certainly was a flex.' Rep. Angie Craig (D-MN) questioned whether a single-commissioner CFTC had the capability to police prediction markets given proposed budget cuts. Chairman Johnson closed by stating: 'Courts are acting in this space. The commission is acting in this space. I do not think that this committee, Congress, should be silent. We have an obligation to drive toward finding out what is the common ground.' Testimony documents are posted at agriculture.house.gov.

items.title: Washington State Court Grants Preliminary Injunction Against Kalshi for Violations of State Gambling Act and Consumer Protection Act
items.facts: King County Superior Court (Washington state) granted a preliminary injunction against Kalshi on July 20, 2026, finding that Kalshi's prediction market contracts likely violate both the Washington Gambling Act and the Consumer Protection Act. The court found that Kalshi's event contracts — covering sports, elections, natural disasters, and other contingent events — constitute gambling under Washington law, which defines gambling as staking or risking something of value upon the outcome of a contest of chance or a future contingent event, and prohibits internet gambling as amended in 2006. The court also ruled that Kalshi's marketing constitutes unfair and deceptive acts or practices under the Consumer Protection Act, citing a Kalshi advertisement in which a user texts about finding 'a way to bet on the NFL even though we live in Washington.' Washington AG Nick Brown filed the underlying complaint on March 27, 2026. The court will issue a final injunction order setting full remedies on August 5, 2026. Washington is reported as the 4th state to obtain a preliminary injunction against Kalshi's sports event contracts, with state regulators and courts prevailing in 19 of 23 such decisions nationally.

items.facts: On July 20, 2026 (filed on public inspection July 17), the FDIC published a Paperwork Reduction Act notice (FR Doc. 2026-14589, 91 FR 45274) requesting 60-day public comment on proposed weekly and quarterly reporting forms for FDIC-supervised Permitted Payment Stablecoin Issuers (PPSIs). Weekly Form PS-01 (for PPSIs with $1 billion or more in total outstanding issuance value or $100 million or more in average daily transaction volume) includes eight schedules covering top holders, top exchanges, trading volume, top counterparties, capital, issuance and redemption, and reserve assets disaggregated by type (cash and deposits, U.S. Treasuries by CUSIP, reverse repurchase agreements, money market mutual funds, and other instruments). Weekly Form PS-01a (smaller PPSIs) has three schedules. Quarterly Form PS-02 covers income statement, balance sheet, off-balance sheet items, capital and operational backstop, and memoranda including blockchain activity, redemption metrics, and custody activities. The FDIC estimates approximately 30 FDIC-supervised institutions would perform PPSI activities; ongoing weekly reporting burden estimated at 2,080 hours per year and quarterly at 800 hours. The publication confirms the FDIC GENIUS Act implementing final rule was not published as of the July 18, 2026 statutory one-year deadline. Comment period closes September 18, 2026.

items.issuing_body: Federal Reserve Board
items.title: Fed Chair Warsh testifies to House Financial Services: no Federal Reserve bailout for crypto or stablecoins; Fed 'racing' to meet GENIUS Act stablecoin rulemaking deadline; nonbank fintech payment access pressed
items.facts: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh testified before the House Committee on Financial Services on July 14, 2026, as part of the Semiannual Monetary Policy Report (2128 Rayburn House Office Building, 10:00 AM). The official prepared statement focused on price stability, monetary policy, and internal Fed task forces. During the Q&A, Warsh made three statements directly relevant to crypto, stablecoin, and fintech operators: (1) No Federal Reserve bailout for crypto or stablecoins: Pressed by Rep. Brad Sherman on whether the Fed would provide the kind of support it gave money market funds in 2008, Warsh stated 'We do not want to be in the bailout business, full stop.' He added that the Fed would 'do everything we can to mitigate... extraordinary risks' but would not bail out crypto. He did not fully rule out marginal systemic-spillover mitigation. (2) GENIUS Act rulemaking urgency: Warsh told lawmakers the Fed is 'racing' to finalize its portion of the GENIUS Act stablecoin implementing rules ahead of the July 18, 2026 one-year statutory deadline. The deadline has since been confirmed missed (the Federal Register contains no in-scope publication; July 18 is a Saturday; earliest possible publication is Monday July 20). items.title: Arizona Department of Gaming issues cease-and-desist orders to five online gambling operators alleging felony promotion of gambling, illegal control of an enterprise, and money laundering
items.facts: On July 10, 2026, the Arizona Department of Gaming announced it had issued cease-and-desist orders to BetOpenly, Bookmaker, Club WPT Online Poker, Kutt Inc., and Raffle Creator, with each enforcement action alleging conduct giving rise to the felonies of promotion of gambling, illegal control of an enterprise, and money laundering. The Department alleges, among other things, that BetOpenly enabled event wagering and daily fantasy sports contests without the requisite state licenses and facilitated availability to underage Arizonans; that Bookmaker facilitated wagering on horse racing, casino games, and sports betting without an event wagering or advanced deposit wagering provider license; that Club WPT Online Poker enabled Arizonans under 21 to engage in pay-to-play online poker tournaments for prizes while using deceptive 'no purchase necessary' language; that Kutt Inc. allowed Arizona users to deposit money and wager on sports, politics, pop culture and casino-style games in a manner providing prohibited third-party benefit; and that Raffle Creator allowed people under 21 to purchase raffle tickets for prizes without meeting Arizona nonprofit raffle requirements. Notified entities are directed to immediately stop all gambling operations and activities in Arizona and to desist from future illegal gambling operations; the Department states future actions may include criminal charges or civil action against entities, principals, and employees, potential restitution awards, and forfeiture of all monies acquired due to the illegal conduct. Department Director Jackie Johnson said, 'Through these cease-and-desist orders we are putting operators on notice: their conduct runs contrary to Arizona law and they must stop promoting illegal gambling.' All conduct described is alleged by the Department and unadjudicated.

items.facts: On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court of the United States issued its 6-3 opinion in Trump v. Slaughter (No. 25-332), authored by Chief Justice Roberts, overturning Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935). The Court held that the for-cause removal protection in the FTC's enabling statute — and by structural extension the SEC and CFTC, which operate under identical removal provisions — is contrary to the separation of powers under the Constitution. Effective immediately, the President may remove SEC and CFTC commissioners without cause. A companion order in Trump v. Cook (No. 25A312, June 29, 2026) denied a government application to stay a preliminary injunction protecting Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook; the Federal Reserve's statutory structure was not directly addressed by the majority opinion. The opinion is published on the Court's official slip opinion list for October Term 2025.
items.source_label: U.S. Supreme Court — Official Slip Opinion List, October Term 2025 (primary source; retrieved July 3, 2026); Opinion PDF: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/25-322_new_4gcj.pdf

Outstanding disputes included DeFi oversight provisions, stablecoin rewards provisions, AML reporting requirements, and Section 604 (Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act). The bill remains on the Senate Legislative Calendar (General Orders, Calendar No. 423) and is not dead; a floor vote has been pushed to after the July 4 recess at earliest. Multiple trade outlets reported prediction market passage odds fell from approximately 74% approximately one month prior to approximately 48% as of the July 2 reporting date.

items.facts: Delaware and New Jersey have each advanced legislation to ban cryptocurrency ATMs statewide, citing fraud losses. Delaware's HB 441 passed the House; it would require existing kiosks to go dark upon enactment and be physically removed within 90 days. New Jersey's S-2141 cleared the Senate Commerce Committee unanimously.
items.source_label: The Defiant (reporting the Delaware and New Jersey crypto-ATM ban bills)
items.relevant_to: crypto-ATM/kiosk operators, payment processors, compliance vendors

items.issuing_body: Gary Gensler (amicus) — U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
items.title: Gensler files Sixth Circuit amicus arguing sports prediction markets are not 'swaps'
items.facts: On 2026-06-11, former CFTC and SEC chair Gary Gensler filed an amicus brief with the Sixth Circuit in KalshiEx LLC v. Schuler, arguing that sports-event prediction-market contracts fall outside the statutory definition of a 'swap' under Dodd-Frank and are therefore not within the CFTC's exclusive jurisdiction.
items.source_label: The Defiant (reporting the Gensler Sixth Circuit amicus brief)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms, derivatives exchanges, crypto exchanges

items.issuing_body: State of Wisconsin (Attorney General) — U.S. District Court, W.D. Wis.
items.title: Wisconsin moves to block sports event-contract trading on Coinbase, Kalshi, and Robinhood
items.facts: On 2026-06-09, the State of Wisconsin filed a motion for a preliminary injunction seeking to block KalshiEx, Coinbase, and Robinhood from offering sports event-contract trading to people in the state.
items.source_label: DeFi Rate (reporting the Wisconsin preliminary-injunction motion)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms, crypto exchanges, brokerages

items.issuing_body: Coalition for Fair Markets (NADEX, Kalshi, Polymarket/QCX)
items.title: Prediction-market coalition sues Kentucky over 14.25% tax on event-contract trading
items.facts: On 2026-06-12, the Coalition for Fair Markets — comprising Crypto.com's NADEX, Kalshi, and Polymarket's U.S. exchange QCX — filed suit in Franklin Circuit Court to block Kentucky from implementing a 14.25% tax on prediction-market transaction fees set to take effect Jan. 1, 2027.
items.source_label: SBC Americas (reporting the Coalition for Fair Markets filing; first reported by the Associated Press)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms, licensed gaming operators, payment processors

items.issuing_body: Nevada Gaming Control Board
items.title: Nevada gaming regulator seeks to hold Kalshi in contempt over prediction-market geofencing
items.facts: On 2026-06-12 the Nevada Gaming Control Board petitioned the First Judicial District Court in Carson City to find KalshiEx LLC in contempt for allegedly not complying with a May 18 order requiring it to geofence its website so it cannot offer sports-, election-, or entertainment-related event contracts to anyone located in Nevada.
items.source_label: Las Vegas Review-Journal (reporting the Nevada GCB court filing)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms, geolocation/compliance vendors, sportsbooks

items.issuing_body: CFTC
items.title: CFTC sues New Mexico over prediction-market preemption (8th state)
items.facts: On 2026-06-12 the CFTC filed suit against the State of New Mexico, seeking a declaratory judgment that federal law grants it exclusive authority over event contracts and a permanent injunction barring the state from enforcing preempted gaming laws against CFTC registrants. New Mexico joins AZ, CT, IL, NY, MN, RI, and WI.
items.source_label: CFTC Press Release 9251-26
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms, sportsbooks, exchanges, CFTC registrants
